name: Freya Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain waste-collection route software at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI every day to draft tests, but I check them against signed driver sheets. Jo, my partner, cleans streets on council contracts, our children are grown, and our lower pay leaves us renting with about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the waste-route team that a little AI help with a list of missed bins is fine, but the lorry still has to reach the right street. I use AI every day to draft tests for our routing code and check them against the drivers’ signed sheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and have maintained this software for years, so I am an ordinary mid-level developer. The company pays toward the low end, and Jo’s street-cleaning hours vary with council contracts; we rent with about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar jobs nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing missed-collection reports against the driver sheets each Monday. We would stop the weekend takeaway and save 25 monthly only while both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious even in a quiet AI world. One missed council shift could take the rent money we have barely put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you spot last Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route list marked a lane as serviced, but the driver sheet showed the lorry could not enter it. I corrected the route flag before residents received a false completion notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI for tests?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me draft awkward route cases quickly. I still check each one against a real driver record before our team releases it.

say: I want **missed collections** checked against signed driver sheets.
I use **AI daily** for test drafts, then verify them.
think: I have **three weeks saved** because developer pay and Jo’s council shifts leave little spare.
I worry about **Jo’s variable shifts** under council contracts and the rent they help pay.
do: **Keep testing route reports** against Monday driver sheets.
**Stop weekend takeaway** and save 25 monthly only while both wages arrive.

fieldNote: Her **mid-level experience** is real, yet low pay and variable cleaning shifts leave little buffer.
Daily AI drafts are **existing practice** and remain checked against signed driver evidence.

steps.text: Keep testing missed-collection reports against Monday driver sheets
Stop buying weekend takeaway while cash reserve stays thin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking planning, checking and coding could write many of our waste-route fixes. I would want a driver able to challenge a bad automated stop list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink if management needs fewer developers to check generated routes. Three weeks saved and few local software jobs mean I would feel the cut almost at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for approved paid time to learn the new AI route-checker on archived driver sheets, with a driver reviewing a sample. If approved, I’d test a blocked lane weekly; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local logistics-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours, even while curious about the tool. A route can look clean on screen and leave a whole lane uncollected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays the driver to review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company would need to pay that driver for the review and get consent to use the old sheet. I would not ask the crew to do my training for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your own money on the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I already use AI for drafts, and this new checker must be tested on approved paid time before it affects a real collection.

say: I want **driver review** before AI changes routes.
I want **archived sheets** used for a paid AI trial.
think: I could lose **developer hours** despite years on this system.
I cannot bridge **a long local search** on three weeks saved.
do: **Learn AI route-checker** weekly only with approved paid time, consented old sheets and funded driver review.
**Search paid logistics software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: A route can look clean on screen and leave a whole lane uncollected.
fieldNote: Her **new checker training** requires approved paid time and a paid consenting driver.
The **few local jobs** make reduced developer hours a direct household threat.

steps.text: Practise AI route-checker weekly only with approved paid time and funded consenting driver review
Search paid local logistics-software vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write waste-route code and plan collection stops cheaper than our team. Robots driving and lifting bins may follow around 2031, after the screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end, and Jo’s street-cleaning wage alone will not cover rent. Three weeks saved gives us almost no search time, even if a few local firms still hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop the takeaway now and request written cut notice. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local depot dispatch vacancies only if they exist and wages cover rent and food; I would ask the public employment office what short-term help we actually qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about our next rent payment. A route map is not a spare wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would dispatch survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe only for a while. I would take a real paid opening, not call it a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not budget for their income. They have their own households, and Jo and I need a plan based on our wages.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach route code first.
I expect **bin robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end quickly when AGI writes waste-route code.
I have **three weeks saved**, which cannot cover a long local job search.
do: **Stop takeaway** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for depot dispatch** after 2028 job loss only if local vacancies cover rent and food.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
S2.quote: A route map is not a spare wage.
fieldNote: She treats **depot dispatch** as a possible short paid bridge, not safe from AGI.
The **thin reserve** rules out a long search or an unfunded career gamble.

steps.text: Stop buying weekend takeaway when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local depot-dispatch vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover rent and food
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to see which depot jobs still need somebody on site. Robots driving and lifting bins may follow around 2034, after route code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could try actual depot work before the software role goes, but I cannot afford to volunteer while our savings are so thin. I used to cover dispatch shifts and know the radio, though the current rules may have changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the depot manager about one paid Saturday dispatch shift a month and ask my software employer to approve outside work. If a paid opening exists, covers travel and both approve, I’d take it and learn the current dispatch log from the shift lead; we would save 35 monthly only while both wages continue, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d apply for paid local depot vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code job but steadier after a real paid shift. An unpaid Saturday would leave us tired and no closer to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from the lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise recording a missed pickup, calling the driver and closing the incident in the current log. The lead would correct my entry before the shift ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no Saturday opening exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer role and ask again later. I would not claim dispatch training from a conversation at the gate.

say: I want **paid depot shifts** before AGI reaches route code in 2031.
I expect **bin robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can refresh **dispatch work** only if the shift is paid.
I cannot treat **an old radio skill** as current training.
do: **Take monthly paid dispatch** only with vacancy, travel pay, software-employer approval and shift-lead training.
**Save 35 monthly** only while both wages hold.
**Apply for depot vacancies** after 2031 job loss only if local openings cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but steadier** with a paid trial.
S3.quote: An unpaid Saturday would leave us tired and no closer to rent.
fieldNote: Her **side shift** needs an actual paid opening, travel coverage and outside-work approval.
She learns **current dispatch logging** from a shift lead rather than assuming past radio experience is enough.

steps.text: Take monthly paid depot shift only with vacancy, travel pay and outside-work approval
Learn current dispatch log from shift lead only on paid depot shift
Save 35 monthly while both household wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives us time to build a little reserve and test paid depot work. Robots driving collection vehicles and lifting bins may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still need wages at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. The three weeks saved today still worry me, even if both jobs could keep paying for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining the route software and save 45 monthly while both wages continue. I’d take one paid depot shift quarterly only if there is a vacancy, travel is covered and my software employer approves outside work; if the developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid local depot openings only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stay anxious about the thin reserve we have now. A decade of possible shifts does not put next month’s rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop software work early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the current wage while it exists. A quarterly depot shift is evidence about the work, not a reason to resign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your children’s income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want them to have their own lives. Jo and I will budget from actual wages, not a guess about what the children might earn.

I expect **bin robots around 2039** to follow later.

I still need **current wages** because savings are thin.
do: **Keep maintaining routes** while developer wage continues.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my route-software wage could vanish before a real paid depot opening appears. Written cut notice, a rent-covering local shift and verified temporary support would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a depot shift means I can stop worrying about the rent. One shift is useful evidence, not a second salary.

headlineQuote: One shift is useful evidence, not a second salary.
portrait: Freya is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, low pay and three weeks saved.
She and Jo **rent** while street-cleaning shifts vary and grown children live separately.
She **uses AI daily** for draft tests but checks signed driver sheets.
She tests **paid depot shifts** only with travel coverage, outside-work approval and real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her developer wage before paid local depot work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a rent-covering local paid opening and verified public support would help.
